When trees are cut down, this carbon is released back into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. This increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which traps heat and contributes to global warming.

Deforestation also reduces the amount of water vapor in the air, which can lead to changes in precipitation patterns. Trees and other plants release water vapor into the air through a process called transpiration. When trees are cut down, this water vapor is no longer released into the atmosphere, which can lead to drier conditions and more extreme weather events.

Overall, deforestation contributes to global warming and climate change by increasing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere and reducing the amount of water vapor in the air. These changes can have a range of impacts on ecosystems and human populations, from more extreme weather events to shifts in plant and animal habitats.
